1:
Calvin (reformed) states the design: Moses asks for love before he exhorts to obedience. He might have commanded with menace; he chose to lead gently by the sweetness of grace, since what is drawn out by servile fear cannot please God. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) makes the point from the syntax: there is no break in the original, so the command reads straight on from the end of the last chapter, where God has made them as the stars of heaven for multitude. Henry (puritan-evangelical) and Gill (reformed) take that multiplication as the argument, Henry adding that those built up from small beginnings should use the fact upon themselves. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) puts the negative case: a heart destitute of the love of God is empty of all good, so without it there could be neither obedience nor happiness.

What is the charge to be kept? Ellicott renders it keep his keeping, alway being all the days, so that not one is omitted. Henry hears the language of the sanctuary in it, oracles and ordinances entrusted to men who must answer for them — a phrase used of priests, because all Israel was a kingdom of priests; and he ties the halves together, since only obedience flowing from love is acceptable. Calvin observes that the precepts are named over by different words, Moses’ way of signalling that nothing needed to regulate a life was left out, and takes the first as a rail fencing life against error on either hand.

The appeal turns to memory, and the witnesses divide over who is addressed. Keil (grammatical-historical) treats the clause about the children as a verbless parenthesis, best supplied as it is not with your children that I have to do, and takes the excluded party to be the desert-born, not the men who had watched the plagues as boys. Ellicott reckons it precisely: anyone under twenty at the Exodus is still alive, so every man of forty-five would feel the address. Henry pitches it at the elders, those above fifty who could remember the deliverance. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) keeps the imperative simple: to know is to acknowledge and consider, with thankfulness. Calvin, weighing whether know ye governs the noun that follows, holds the word too general to be narrowed to chastisement; Ellicott keeps chastisement and asks only whose — of the Egyptians in wrath, or of Israel in love.

Gill reads the miracles in Egypt as the plagues sent for refusing to let Israel go; Henry sets the two judgments side by side — a country laid waste to force Israel’s enlargement, an army drowned to prevent their re-enslavement — and reads it by Isaiah 43:3, a kingdom spent as ransom rather than a people left undelivered. Wesley notices the tense in destroyed unto this day and takes it of an effect still running, as does Calvin. Of the wilderness Gill says the reference is to the chastisements for murmuring and idolatry rather than the kindnesses, and Calvin that those years are set out compendiously, partly that God’s judgments might alarm and partly that his mercies might draw.

Dathan and Abiram get the longest look. Henry treats the earth swallowing them as mercy to Israel: Reubenites had defied Moses and headed a rebellion that threatened the ruin of a whole people, and deliverance from insurrection at home is as great a kindness as protection from invasion abroad. Gill ties it to the quarrel over the priesthood at Numbers 16. Ellicott turns the verse against a critical argument: Korah’s rebellion cannot be separated from theirs, and its point was the distinction between a Kohathite and a priest, so the writer can hardly have known only the tribe’s priesthood. The section closes on sight, which Ellicott renders as your eyes being the witnesses of all the great working of Jehovah.
8:
Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) draws the inference backwards from the judgments just rehearsed: a God who can execute such things, and may act so again under the same provocation, is to be obeyed — keep his charge, that he may keep you unto everlasting life. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that the noun is singular, so what is enjoined is one course of action rather than a list of details, and reads go in and possess as completing the conquest piece by piece. Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets out the two halves: obedience gets possession and keeps it. Moses does not teach them the art of war, how to draw the bow or hold ranks; their religion, while they are true to it, is their strength. Gill (reformed) adds that entering the land and continuing long in it were two different things.

Then comes the comparison with Egypt, and the odd phrase about the foot. Clarke explains it from the ground: rain scarcely falls in Egypt, and the Nile supplies the want, but where the flood does not reach, water is ponded and led off in streamlets, and a man opening a channel with a small mattock banks the mould against its side with his foot so the water is not spilt before it arrives. He adds a treadle engine still used in the east, tipped into the river by a man plunging it with his foot. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the labour more broadly — fetching water, digging furrows with the foot, working machines with the feet — and observes that the Nile often failed in part, and that its mud soon hardened and wanted watering again. Ellicott leaves the choice open between carrying the water and channelling it by foot.

Canaan is the opposite case. Gill points out that a land of hills and valleys cannot be watered by a river’s overflow as a flat country can, names its heights and valleys as what makes it pleasant for prospects, and prefers its rain on grounds of health: the damps off the Nile were unwholesome, and its summer flood shut the Egyptians indoors for weeks. Wesley itemises the advantage — easier, coming without pains; pleasanter, not confining a man to his house; safer, being free of the mud; and more certain, the former and latter rain being promised in their seasons on condition of obedience, a condition that looks like a clog and is in fact a benefit, binding a people by their own interest to what their happiness depends on. Henry draws the contrast sharply: while Egypt is ditching up to the knees in mud, Israel may sit still and leave the watering to God, whose rain is called the river of God, perhaps in contempt of the river Egypt was so proud of.

The last clause interests them most. Ellicott gives it literally as a land which the LORD seeketh, sets it beside the land God had espied for his people at Ezekiel 20:6, and finds it hard not to hear the better country behind it; he also records the Jewish objection that God causes it to rain where no man is, so that seeking out a land can hardly be unique. Keil (grammatical-historical) keeps it concrete: God inquires after this land, his eyes are on it from one year’s beginning to its end, and that dependence is exactly what fits it for a people meant to live wholly to their God. Gill allows a general providence over the earth and a particular care here, this being the place chosen for his worship. Henry and Wesley then reach independently for the same argument from the land’s later state: its fruitfulness was never the soil’s but the blessing’s, so a barren Canaan is what Psalms 107:34 threatened, and confirms the word rather than embarrassing it.
13:
Ellicott (grammatical-historical) marks the turn: here begins the formal sanction of the charge, a declaration of rewards and punishments, a characteristic feature of the Law which he traces through Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 into the close of the Sermon on the Mount. Keil (grammatical-historical) says the same structurally: the peculiarity of the land leads Moses to end this part of the discourse with a blessing and a curse. Ellicott also keeps a Jewish gloss that serving with all the heart points to prayer, since in Babylon Israel had no other service left, though he allows the words a wider reach.

The blessing is rain, and Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) explains why the two seasons matter. The former rain fell about November at sowing and prepared the ground; the latter about April, when the corn was up, and filled the ears. Rain rarely fell otherwise, so without the first there is no growth and without the second no harvest. From God promising it on obedience and threatening to withhold it on disobedience, Clarke concludes flatly that this is not general providence but particular. Ellicott dates them to the ninth and first months from Joel 2:23, and repeats a reading that thou shalt gather in may carry a promise of its own — thou, and not thine enemies, as at Isaiah 62:8. Henry (puritan-evangelical) adds that in due season means neither wanting when the ground calls for it nor coming in excess, and takes it as standing for every seasonable mercy. Gill (reformed) notes the grass is given for the cattle so that they may serve man; Ellicott, on being full, preserves the observation that this is a further blessing belonging to the food in a man’s inward parts, since one may eat and not be satisfied. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) turns it: godliness has the promise of this life, yet God’s favour puts more gladness into the heart than corn and wine and oil.

Then the warning, and Gill sees the trap in the blessing itself: watching how the heavens govern the fruitfulness of the earth, a man may slide into worshipping the host of them, helped on by the nations round about and by arguments from ancestral tradition, antiquity, and the sheer number of worshippers. Ellicott puts the moment precisely: take heed when you are satisfied. Calvin (reformed) hears in the repeated command an indirect charge against our proneness to superstition — nothing is easier than to fall into the snare — and has no patience with anyone who lulls himself into security where God exhorts to solicitude. Turning aside, he insists, is no small excess: whoever declines to a corrupted worship has fallen away from the true God, however light men count it and however firmly they shelter behind good intentions, as though God were not free to refuse what they obtrude on him. Henry adds the sting — a little care would have prevented it, and that will aggravate the ruin.

The threat reverses everything just promised. Keil states it plainly: the wrath of the LORD would burn, he would shut up the heaven so that no rain fell and the earth yielded nothing, and they would speedily perish. Wesley supplies the picture behind the phrase, heaven as the storehouse of Job 38:22 where God lays up his treasures of rain, with doors he opens and shuts. Gill says why idolatry above all provokes him, as contrary to his very being as well as to his will. Henry sets the three consequences in order: the anger provoked, and who knows its power; the good things withdrawn; and the evil brought, perishing quickly from a good land. The better the land, he adds, the more grievous to perish from it, and its goodness is no security once its inhabitants are ripe for ruin.
18:
Ellicott (grammatical-historical) begins with the joint. The word rendered therefore is a simple and, so the sentence can be read straight on from the threat before it — ye will perish quickly from off the good land, and ye will lay these my words to your hearts — and he records the Jewish comment that they would remember them in captivity if not before. He then declines the reading he has made attractive: the promise of multiplied days a few lines later shows it cannot be the primary sense, and the sadder one is an application suggested by the event rather than the grammar. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) does no more than point back to the earlier place where the same charge was given, which is itself the observation — nothing here is new.

What is asked for is depth before display. Calvin (reformed) takes laying up in the heart to mean hiding deeply, and notes that where soul is added alongside, the heart carries the mind and the understanding, so the demand is for the Law both impressed on the intellect and embraced with sincere affection. Gill (reformed) says the same in three motions — treasure the laws in the mind, retain them in the memory, cherish a cordial affection for them — and names the use: an antidote against apostasy and idolatry. Henry (puritan-evangelical) organises the whole verse under three rules, and Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) gives the identical three almost word for word. Let the heart be filled with the word, as a store-house to be drawn on for every occasion, since good practice in the conversation cannot be expected without good thoughts and affections and principles within. Let the eyes be fixed on it, bound on the hand which is always in view and set as frontlets between the eyes, which cannot be avoided. Let the tongue be employed about it, and above all with children, who must be taught the service of God as the one thing needful.

Calvin presses the sign and the frontlets harder than anyone. The point of wearing the precepts, he says, was that God should constantly meet them and rouse their senses; he had no regard to the bands themselves, but appointed them to stand where ornaments stand, so that a people might learn to take their chief delight in meditating on the Law. That purpose, he argues, is what condemns two abuses of it: the ambition that hunts a reputation for holiness by fringes and finery, and the grosser error of supposing an outward dress discharges a duty to God. Writing the words on gate and doorpost serves the same end, because minds prone to vanity and pulled about by innumerable distractions need such stays to hold them; and the command to speak of them sitting, walking, lying down and rising up is there because what is once learnt is soon lost without diligent exercise.

Both the reformed and the puritan reading end at the same place, in the next generation. Calvin observes that the charge is not only for each man’s own advantage but for teaching his children, which is how the Law would be kept in vigour by an unbroken succession. Henry reaches it by another road: great pains must be taken to acquaint children early with the word, more than are spent on the rules of decency or the calling they will live by, and nothing contributes more to the continuance of religion in a nation than the good education of its children — if the seed be holy, it is the substance of a land. Henry also turns the frontlets into a rule of conduct rather than a rule of dress, laying God’s judgments before us as the guide of the way and the rule of the work.
21:
Ellicott (grammatical-historical) stops on a pronoun. The land was sworn to the fathers to give them, not to give you, and he reports the Jewish inference drawn from that — that the resurrection of the dead is taught here, since men long dead are still to receive what was promised. He will not brush it aside: were it a Christian’s remark it would be called fanciful, but it is a Jew’s, and the Jewish conviction that the promises to Abraham and Isaac and Jacob will be literally kept, on no other ground than God’s word, is a fact whatever one makes of it. He points to Acts 7:5 as singularly pointed on the same difficulty: God gave Abraham no inheritance in the land, not so much as to set his foot on, and promised it to him and to his seed nonetheless. Gill (reformed) keeps to the plain sense, long life being a desirable blessing promised to obedience, and Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the measure of it as the heaven’s own continuance over the earth.

The condition is stated twice over, and Gill insists on the difference between knowing the commandments and doing them: what is asked is not a theory or a notional knowledge but practice. Ellicott takes the two verbs of the condition in turn and lets a Jewish commentator answer both. To walk in all his ways is glossed, he is compassionate and thou shalt be compassionate, he showeth mercies and thou shalt show mercies — a comment Ellicott calls worthy of the New Testament, adding only that what follows shows the need of a mediator. To cleave unto him raises the sharper question, whether a man may speak so of a consuming fire at all; the answer given is to cleave to wise men and their disciples, and it shall be as though one cleaved to him. Ellicott translates that into his own idiom without embarrassment, as being followers of one who follows Christ, and as receiving the sent one and so the sender.

Then the promise of ground. Gill notes that the nations are driven out by little and little, all seven of them, to make room; and on the sweeping clause about the sole of the foot he and Wesley agree in refusing the unlimited reading, that wherever the foot of an Israelite falls the ground becomes his. Both hold the promise bounded by the borders the verse itself goes on to name, and Wesley maps them — the wilderness of Sin on the south, Lebanon on the north, Euphrates on the east, the midland sea on the west — distinguishing possession from dominion and making both conditional on obedience. He adds that their sins cut them short of it, and that Solomon reached it. Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reaches the same conclusion from the other end: the promise was fulfilled in Solomon’s reign, notwithstanding all the provocations between, since he reigned from the river to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt. Ellicott only notes the clause returning at Joshua 1:3.

The last promise is of terror rather than territory, and here the two readings part. Gill argues that no man able to stand cannot mean a single man, since nobody could have feared one champion against six hundred thousand fighting men; it must mean no people or nation, however much greater and mightier. Ellicott, taking the Jewish distinction that fear falls on those near and dread on those far off, reads the clause as reaching much further — upon all the earth that ye shall tread upon — and finds it answered in the terror that ran through a whole empire at Esther 8:2. The territorial promise is thus kept narrow by one set of witnesses and the promise of dread let out wide by another, in consecutive verses.
26:
Henry (puritan-evangelical) treats this as the close of the whole exhortation and admires the management of it. Moses reduces every argument he has made to two words, the blessing and the curse, which are the rewards and punishments as they stand in the promises and threatenings — the great sanctions of the law, taking hold of hope and fear, those two handles of the soul by which it is caught and held and managed. Setting them before the people meant three things: explaining them, so they might see how desirable the one was and how dreadful the other; confirming them from his commission, so the blessing should not be taken for a fool’s paradise nor the curse for a bugbear; and charging them to choose. Henry notes how fair that is in a man who had been accused at Numbers 16:14 of putting out the eyes of those he led.

Calvin (reformed) reaches the same pair from the other side and uses almost the same words: the doctrine so far delivered is sealed by hope and fear, since obedience will not lose its labour nor rejection go unpunished. To say that a blessing and a curse are set before them is to say that Moses is not merely telling them what is right but announcing that the reward is prepared and the punishment at hand. Calvin then notices something easy to pass over. Moses insists both that God is the Author of the Law, a faithful rewarder and a severe judge, and that it is Moses who commands after God; the second point is there because men are proud enough to want to fly above the clouds and hear God directly, when he chooses to be heard through the servants he speaks by. Gill (reformed) keeps the terms concrete: blessing in body and estate, in family and flock, in town and country; and cursing in basket and store, going out and coming in, and not in this world only. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) records that a Jewish division of the book opens here, and renders the pair without the articles — blessing and cursing, the one if you obey and the other if you do not.

Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) turns the verse into an argument, the sharpest thing in the chapter. If God had not put it in this people’s power either to obey or to disobey, could such precepts have been given at all with such promises and threatenings attached? Men who are not free agents can neither be punished for disobedience nor in any sense rewarded for obedience. He presses it with an illustration: a stone earns no reward for tending toward the centre in obedience to gravitation, and no guilt if in falling back it takes away a man’s life. A self-determining will, he holds, is declared throughout Scripture, cannot be forced by anything short of omnipotence, and is never forced by God even so; the terms are obey, since God is always ready to assist, and live, or refuse that help and die.

The other witnesses do not answer him, and the chapter does not settle it; what they do instead is fix the alternative more exactly. Gill observes that everyone was called to consider the matter, since it concerned them all, and reads the blessing and the curse as the law under two aspects rather than two dispensations. Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) fastens on the rival gods being ones the people have not known: no acquaintance with them, and no experience of their power or wisdom or goodness, such as they have had of God’s. Henry sets the whole down as terms honestly published, and finishes on the formula that it shall be well with the righteous and ill with the wicked.
29:
Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) begins with the verb: the Hebrew is thou shalt give, that is, pronounce or cause to be pronounced. Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reports the Targums, one rendering the nouns as those that bless and those that curse, another that the blessing was said with faces turned toward Gerizim and the cursing toward Ebal — evidence, he says, for the antiquity of the traditional reading. Calvin (reformed) explains why the people had to say it themselves. Had God declared his will through the Levites alone, they should have listened with reverence; but each man testifying with his own mouth what the Levites dictate turns assent into a ratification. He also sees why the ceremony waits until they are in the land: the sight of the country confirms it, as though they had been brought into court to make a covenant. Henry (puritan-evangelical) notes that Moses here appoints the proclamation to be made publicly on the two hills.

Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) goes at the names. Gerizim he derives from a root meaning to cut down, so that it would mean the fellers or reapers, a name earned by fertility; for Ebal no Hebrew root is found, but a cognate carries the sense of rough and rugged, and of a mountain of white stones, a name earned by barrenness. On that reading he builds an argument: God so superintends this land that nothing changes in it but by his counsel, its fertility always the consequence of obedience and its barrenness the proof of departure. Travellers agree, he says, that one hill is fruitful and the other bare, with Shechem in the valley between; and he presses further, holding Judea naturally dry and stony, so that its carrying so vast a population was a work of particular providence. Calvin adds that the two stand opposite each other, so the divided people could answer one another.

Then the geography, which is evidence. Ellicott calls where the sun goeth down a memorable phrase, since it attests the speaker’s position east of Jordan over against Jericho: travellers on that spot have watched the sun set exactly in the gap between the two mountains. He also corrects plains of Moreh to oaks or terebinths. Gill (reformed) places the hills in Samaria and corrects a rabbinic claim that Israel reached them as soon as they crossed Jordan: they lie some sixty miles from Jericho. Wesley reads over against as looking toward Gilgal at a distance, then makes the point that matters most: Moreh was among the first places Abram came to, so sending the tribes there recalled the promise made on that ground. Ellicott arrives independently, noting that it was by the oak of Moreh that God first told Abram his seed would inherit this land, at Genesis 12:6.

Calvin hears the closing question as an assertion: the interrogative is ordinary Hebrew, but here affirms more vehemently than a plain statement, because Moses is putting confidence into people whose incredulity had survived even the conquest of the Amorites and Bashan. The promise that they shall pass over becomes the ground of the exhortation, since the land is inherited for the purpose of keeping the Law. Gill says the same of the title: the gift is warrant enough, and the closing charge is repeated because their continuance hangs on it. Ellicott marks the seam: the exposition of the people’s relation to God ends here, and what follows takes the land as the seat of worship, then of the kingdom, then as the sphere of rules forming a distinctive character — a structure he says deserves attention because some assign these chapters to a later hand. Henry closes on the gospel: men who have broken the law stand under its curse with no remedy in themselves, and are set once more between blessing and curse.
